results.title: Assessing the utility of natural language processing for detecting postoperative complications from free medical text - PMC
results.content: In addition, the model performance approached that of manual curation and thereby offers a potential pathway for complete real-time coverage of postoperative complications across surgical procedures based on natural language processing assessment of electronic health record free medical text. The hypothesis was that NLP models would be able to detect the target PCs within 30 days of the primary surgical procedure with a performance comparable to manual curation and outperform structured administrative data. The cases within the test data set (*Fig. 1*) with a registered ICD-10 code of relevance within 30 days of a surgical procedure were used to compare the performance of administrative data with the NLP algorithms. Additional performance metrics in terms of sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and negative predictive value (NPV), as well as thresholds for both the SAM and HITL approaches, were determined for the test data set (compared with manual curation as the gold standard). *Table 3* lists performance metrics for the NLP and administrative data for detection of the studied PCs. For the NLP approach, an ROCAUC of 0.989 for UTI, 0.993 for pneumonia, 0.992 for sepsis, and 0.998 for septic shock was achieved. Performance metrics for administrative data, the stand-alone model (SAM) approach, and the human-in-the-loop approach (HITL) (where all cases with model-determined probability of the given complication existing in the chart note exceeding an F2 score optimized threshold are forwarded to human extraction). In one study, Jones *et al*.17 developed an NLP tool to identify the clinical assertion of pneumonia from emergency department notes and compared the performance of the NLP tool with manual chart review—the NLP model demonstrated a sensitivity of 0.72 (training) and 0.55 (validation), as well as a PPV of 0.89 (training) and 0.71 (validation). Compared with the study by Jones *et al*.17 for identifying pneumonia, the models in the present study perform similarly, with a sensitivity of 0.833, a specificity of 0.986, a PPV of 0.485, and an NPV of 0.997 (the SAM approach), with PPV optimization being possible through the HITL approach. In a clinical setting, the NLP models could be directly implemented into EHR systems and serve as a useful aid by flagging patients in real time (EHRs) with potential PCs upon discharge, allowing for extraction of positive cases through the HITL approach and thus increasing the quality of administrative data.

results.title: Addressing Measurement Error in Random Forests Using Quantitative Bias Analysis
results.content: First, we assessed the impact of misclassification (i.e., measurement error of categorical variables) of predictors on random-forest model performance (e.g., accuracy, sensitivity) and variable importance (mean decrease in accuracy) using data from the National Comorbidity Survey Replication (2001–2003). We assessed the impact of misclassification of mental and substance use disorders on random-forest model performance and variable importance using NCS-R validation data for these disorders and quantitative bias analysis. The entire process (i.e., sampling from the beta distributions for sensitivity and specificity, calculating PPV and NPV, reclassifying individual records in the data set to generate a new data set, conducting random-forest analyses, and assessing model performance and variable importance) was repeated 10,000 times to create a distribution of model performance metrics and variable importance values. results.title: Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV and Accuracy :
results.content: Positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) are also statistical measures used in medical research to evaluate the accuracy of a diagnostic test or screening tool. **PPV and NPV depend on the prevalence of the disease in the population being tested.** When the prevalence of the disease is low, even highly specific and sensitive tests can produce a high number of false positives, resulting in a low PPV. PPV and NPV, on the other hand, are measures of the predictive value of the test in a specific population, which takes into account the prevalence of the disease in that population. Sensitivity and specificity are measures of the overall performance of the test, while PPV and NPV are measures of the predictive value of the test in a specific population. Other measures, such as sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value, may also be needed to provide a more complete picture of the diagnostic accuracy of the test.

results.title: Statistics - Sensitivity Specificity PPV NPV - GP Exams
results.content: * **NPV**  A high NPV means that a negative test result is a strong indicator that the patient does not have the disease. + **Sensitivity:** This is the ability of a test to correctly identify those with the disease (true positives). High PPV means that when the test is positive, there’s a high probability that the patient actually has the disease. + **Specificity:** This is the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease (true negatives). A high NPV means that when the test is negative, it’s very likely that the patient does not have the disease. + **High Sensitivity:** If the test has 95% sensitivity, it means that out of 100 patients who have the disease, 95 will test positive (true positives), and 5 will test negative (false negatives). + **High Specificity:** If the test has 95% specificity, it means that out of 100 people who do not have the disease, 95 will correctly test negative (true negatives), and 5 will incorrectly test positive (false positives).
